present.explain: A French verb changes its form for who does it: je mange (I eat), tu manges (you eat), il or elle mange (he or she eats), nous mangeons (we eat). Many of the forms sound alike and are spelled apart: mange, manges and mangent all sound the same. Some common verbs change more: je bois, il boit, nous buvons; je veux, il veut, nous voulons. French always says who: je, tu, il, elle, nous.
present.why: The word for who does it is never left out, because so many forms sound the same: [[je mange]] and [[tu manges]] are only told apart by je and tu.

examples.text: Tu bois du café et je bois du thé.
examples.means: You drink coffee and I drink tea.
examples.literal: You drink some coffee and I drink some tea.

contrasts.says: After vouloir, pouvoir or devoir the second verb stays in its basic form: je veux manger, never je veux mange.
English adds -s for he and she; French changes the verb for every person, often only in writing.

mistakes.why: With je, it's bois.
With nous, the verb ends in -ons.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every French noun is a le word or a la word, and the little words with it match: le téléphone, un café; la table, une clé. Before a vowel, le and la both become l': l'eau. Endings give hints but not rules (le lait, la clé), so learn each noun with its le or la.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the words around it follow: [[le]] téléphone but [[la]] table, [[mon]] café but [[ma]] clé, [[ce]] livre but [[cette]] clé.

examples.text: Le téléphone est sur la table.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.text: Un thé avec du lait, s'il vous plaît.
examples.literal: A tea with some milk, please.

examples.means: The water is on the table.
examples.literal: The water is on the table.

examples.text: La clé est dans ma poche.
examples.means: The key is in my pocket.
examples.literal: The key is in my pocket.

contrasts.says: English has one the and one a for every noun; French has le or la, un or une, by the noun.
mon and ma follow the noun the same way: mon café, ma clé.

mistakes.why: téléphone is a le word: learn it as le téléphone.

mistakes.wrong: Le eau est sur la table.
mistakes.why: Before a vowel, le and la run into the noun: l'eau.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

partitive.explain: For some of something you don't count, French says du with le words and de l' before a vowel: du café, du lait, de l'eau (de la with la words, as in de la limonade). English often says nothing at all: Je bois du café is I drink coffee. After ne … pas, what you don't have, drink or eat takes plain de, as it does after beaucoup: Je n'ai pas de lait, beaucoup de café; after être it stays: Ce n'est pas du thé.
partitive.why: French doesn't leave a noun bare the way English does: where English says I drink coffee, French says I drink [[du]] café, some coffee. du is de and le run together.

examples.text: Il boit du thé avec du lait.
examples.literal: He drinks some tea with some milk.

examples.means: I drink a lot of coffee.
examples.literal: I drink a lot of coffee.

contrasts.says: du goes with le words and de la with la words; before a vowel, both are de l'.
After ne … pas, du becomes de: pas de café.
English often says nothing before coffee or water; French always has du, de la or de l'.

mistakes.why: French needs du before the drink.
de and le always run together: du.
Before a vowel it's de l'.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

negation.explain: ne goes before the verb and pas after it: Je ne bois pas de café, Elle ne vient pas. Before a vowel, ne becomes n': Le thé n'est pas prêt, Je n'ai pas de lait. With a second verb, ne … pas goes around the first: Je ne peux pas lire. In everyday speech ne is often dropped (Je bois pas), but it's always written.
negation.why: English puts not after a helper (I do not drink); French puts [[ne]] and [[pas]] around the verb itself: Je [[ne]] bois [[pas]].

examples.text: Je ne bois pas de lait.
Je ne peux pas lire le livre.

contrasts.says: After ne … pas, du and un become de: pas de café, pas de voiture.
English adds do or does; French has no helper, only ne and pas around the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Je ne bois de lait pas.
mistakes.right: Je ne bois pas de lait.
mistakes.why: pas comes right after the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Le thé ne est pas prêt.
mistakes.why: Before a vowel, ne becomes n'.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: The everyday way to ask yes or no is to keep the sentence as it is and raise your voice at the end: Tu es prêt? Le téléphone est ici? A question word goes first, with the verb straight after it: Où est la voiture? Qu'est-ce que starts a question with what: Qu'est-ce que je peux faire? Written French puts a small space before ?, which the app adds for you.
question.why: French needs no word like English do: [[Tu bois]] du café? is a question by your voice alone.

examples.text: Tu ne bois pas de café?

contrasts.says: English puts is or do first; spoken French keeps the order and lets your voice ask.

mistakes.why: After où, the verb comes next.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: mon (my) goes before a le word and ma before a la word: mon téléphone, ma clé. ton and ta (your, to someone you say tu to) work the same way: ton livre, ta clé. Before a la word that starts with a vowel it's mon and ton again: mon amie. With a plural noun it's mes and tes.
possessive.why: my and your follow the noun, not the owner: a woman says [[mon]] téléphone, and a man says [[ma]] clé.

examples.text: Mon téléphone est dans ma poche.
examples.means: My phone is in my pocket.
examples.literal: My phone is in my pocket.

examples.text: Ta clé est sur la table.
examples.means: Your key is on the table.
examples.literal: Your key is on the table.

contrasts.says: mon, ma follow le and la: le café, mon café; la clé, ma clé.
For someone's, French says de: le livre de ma mère, my mother's book.

mistakes.why: clé is a la word: ma clé.
ma takes the place of la.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

modal.explain: After vouloir (want), pouvoir (can) and devoir (have to), the next verb stays in its basic form, the one ending in -er, -ir or -re: Je veux manger, Tu peux lire ça?, Je dois travailler. Only the first verb changes for who does it, and nothing goes between them: no word for to.
modal.why: [[Je veux]] already says I want, so the second verb stays plain: [[Je veux manger]], never je veux mange.

examples.means: We want to have a coffee.
examples.literal: We want to drink a coffee.
She wants to drink some tea.

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the form for who (veux, veut, voulons); the second never does.
English puts to between them (want to eat); French puts nothing: je veux manger.

mistakes.why: After veux, the basic form.

mistakes.wrong: Nous voulons à boire un café.
mistakes.why: Nothing goes between vouloir and the next verb.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

de.explain: de joins two nouns where English uses 's: le livre de ma mère (the book of my mother: my mother's book), la clé de ma voiture (the key to my car). French has no 's. de and le run together as du.
de.why: English says my mother's book; French turns it round: le livre [[de]] ma mère, the book of my mother.

examples.text: C'est le livre de ma mère.
examples.literal: It's the book of my mother.

examples.text: Il a la clé de ma voiture?
examples.means: Does he have the key to my car?
examples.literal: He has the key of my car?

examples.text: C'est le téléphone de ton père.
examples.literal: It's the phone of your father.

contrasts.says: English uses 's or puts the nouns side by side; French uses de.
The same de, with le run into it, makes du: some.

mistakes.right: C'est le livre de ma mère.
mistakes.why: French has no 's: the book of my mother.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: ce goes before a le word and cette before a la word, for this or that: ce livre, cette clé. Before a le word that starts with a vowel it's cet: cet hôtel. With a plural noun it's ces. Where English chooses between this and that, French usually just says ce.
demonstrative.why: ce follows the noun like le and la do: [[ce]] livre, [[cette]] clé.

examples.text: Cette clé est dans ma poche.
examples.means: This key is in my pocket.
examples.literal: This key is in my pocket.

contrasts.says: ce with le words, cette with la words, the way le and la go.

mistakes.why: clé is a la word: cette clé.
cet is only before a vowel.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

vous.explain: vous is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, someone older, or anyone you'd be formal with, and it's also you to more than one person. Its verb usually ends in -ez (vous êtes, vous faites and vous dites are the exceptions): Vous savez où c'est?, Vous allez à la maison?, Vous voulez un café? tu is for someone you know well, a child, or a friend.
vous.why: French splits English you in two: [[tu]] for one person you know, [[vous]] for anyone else, and the verb follows: tu sais, [[vous savez]].

examples.text: Vous savez où est la voiture?
examples.means: Do you know where the car is?
examples.literal: You know where is the car?

contrasts.says: vous has its own form, usually ending in -ez: vous savez, vous voulez, vous allez; but vous êtes.
English has one you; French says tu or vous by who you're talking to.

mistakes.why: With vous, savoir is savez.
After pour, tu becomes toi; vous stays vous.

source.note: Written with the French lessons, open to correction.

elision.explain: Some short words lose their final vowel before a word beginning with a vowel sound: je + ai becomes j'ai; la + eau becomes l'eau; ne + est becomes n'est; de + eau becomes d'eau. The apostrophe marks that join. It is required in these examples. A mute h allows the same join, but an aspirate h blocks it; the spelling h alone does not tell you which kind it is.
elision.why: The apostrophe replaces the missing vowel: [[j'ai]], not je ai. l'eau is still a feminine noun even though l' hides le or la.

examples.means: The water is on the table.
examples.literal: The water is on the table.

contrasts.says: Both le and la become l' before a vowel; the noun keeps its gender.
English contractions such as I'm work differently: learn the French joins from the French words.

mistakes.why: je loses its e before ai.

mistakes.wrong: La eau est sur la table.
mistakes.why: la loses its a before eau.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.explain: qui asks who, où where and comment how. Qu'est-ce que introduces a question with what. A question word does not force one fixed word order: Où est la voiture? has the noun after est, while Comment je peux aider? keeps je before peux. Both are everyday questions. The question word tells you what kind of answer is wanted.
question-word.why: In [[Comment]] je peux aider?, the missing information is how to help. French needs no extra do to ask.

contrasts.says: Rising intonation can ask yes or no; a question word requests a person, place or other missing information.
The question keeps peux + infinitive: Comment je peux aider?

mistakes.why: The question still uses the je form peux.
la voiture takes est.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

tonic-pronoun.explain: After a preposition, the person addressed is toi: avec toi (with you), chez toi (at your house). Before the verb as its subject, use tu: Tu viens. The person is the same; the role in the sentence changes the form. vous keeps the same spelling after a preposition, as in pour vous.
tonic-pronoun.why: [[tu]] does the action; after avec or chez, use [[toi]].

examples.means: I want to be with you.
examples.literal: I want to be with you.

examples.means: My dad is at your house.
examples.literal: My dad is at your place.

contrasts.says: The polite or plural form vous does not change after pour: pour vous.
English uses you in both roles; French distinguishes tu and toi.

mistakes.why: avec takes toi, not the subject form tu.
chez takes toi.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: For a direct instruction, leave out the subject pronoun and use the command form: Appelle ton père (call your dad). The command to someone you address as vous is Appelez: Appelez le médecin, s'il vous plaît. A regular -er command to tu has no final -s (appelle), except right before y or en, which come in later lessons. Keep the address consistent: the polite appelez goes with s'il vous plaît.
imperative.why: An instruction addresses the listener directly, so [[Appelle]] already says what to do; it has no tu in front.

examples.means: Give your dad a quick call.

examples.text: Appelez le médecin, s'il vous plaît.

contrasts.says: A statement says who acts; an instruction uses the command form without its subject pronoun.
Appelez is the polite or plural command, and s'il vous plaît matches it.

mistakes.why: The familiar command is appelle; the polite or plural form is spelled appelez.

mistakes.wrong: Appelez le médecin, s'il vous plais.
mistakes.right: Appelez le médecin, s'il vous plaît.
mistakes.why: The set expression uses plaît, whose subject is il.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

conditional.explain: je voudrais means I'd like. Use it to make a request more polite than je veux (I want): Je voudrais un rendez-vous avec le médecin. voudrais is a form of vouloir, not a new verb. For now, learn this useful request as it is.
conditional.why: [[Je voudrais]] softens the request; the speaker is asking for an appointment.

examples.text: Je voudrais un rendez-vous avec le médecin.
examples.means: I'd like an appointment with the doctor.
examples.literal: I would like an appointment with the doctor.

contrasts.says: Je veux means I want; Je voudrais means I'd like and is a politer request.

mistakes.why: With je, this form is voudrais, ending in -s.
rendez-vous is masculine, so it takes un.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time.explain: à introduces the time of an event: à deux heures means at two o'clock. The written -s in heures marks more than one hour. You can put the time first or last: À deux heures, je dois travailler; Je dois travailler à deux heures. Moving the time does not change je dois into a different order.
time.why: French counts the hours: [[deux heures]]. English says two o'clock.

examples.text: J'ai un rendez-vous à deux heures.
examples.means: I have an appointment at two o'clock.
examples.literal: I have an appointment at two hours.

examples.text: À deux heures, je dois travailler.
examples.means: At two o'clock, I have to work.
examples.literal: At two hours, I have to work.

examples.text: Mon rendez-vous est à deux heures.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: My appointment is at two hours.

contrasts.says: deux heures is two o'clock when naming a clock time.
Putting the time first leaves the subject before its verb: À deux heures, je dois travailler.

mistakes.wrong: Mon rendez-vous est à deux heure.
mistakes.right: Mon rendez-vous est à deux heures.
mistakes.why: More than one hour takes written -s.

mistakes.wrong: À deux heures, je doit travailler.
mistakes.right: À deux heures, je dois travailler.
mistakes.why: Moving the time does not change the form used with je: dois.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

infinitive-link.explain: In Il n'a pas d'argent pour payer, pour payer says what the money would be used for. pour is followed by the infinitive payer, not a conjugated form such as paie. This is not a rule to put pour before every infinitive: some verbs require à or de, and vouloir, pouvoir and devoir take a bare infinitive. Learn a verb together with its link.
infinitive-link.why: [[pour payer]] answers what the money is for. The second verb stays in its basic form.

examples.text: Il n'a pas d'argent pour payer.
examples.means: He doesn't have any money to pay with.
examples.literal: He doesn't have any money for paying.

contrasts.says: pouvoir takes no preposition before its infinitive: Je peux payer.
English to does not always become the same French word. The construction decides whether there is a link.

mistakes.wrong: Il n'a pas d'argent pour paie.
mistakes.right: Il n'a pas d'argent pour payer.
mistakes.why: After pour, use the infinitive payer.
After peux, use payer without a preposition.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

indirect-question.explain: ce que means what when it introduces the thing someone says or does inside a larger sentence: Vous comprenez ce que je dis? The embedded part keeps je before dis. Likewise, Je ne comprends pas ce que je dois faire says I don't understand what I have to do. Qu'est-ce que belongs to a direct question; it does not replace ce que in these embedded clauses.
indirect-question.why: The whole sentence asks whether you understand. [[ce que je dis]] names what there is to understand.

examples.text: Vous comprenez ce que je dis?
examples.means: Do you understand what I'm saying?

examples.text: Je ne comprends pas ce que je dois faire.
examples.means: I don't understand what I have to do.
examples.literal: I don't understand what I have to do.

contrasts.says: A direct question can start Qu'est-ce que; inside these sentences, use ce que.
Both languages keep I/je before the verb inside what I say/ce que je dis.

mistakes.wrong: Vous comprend ce que je dis?
mistakes.right: Vous comprenez ce que je dis?
mistakes.why: With vous, use comprenez.

mistakes.wrong: Vous comprenez ce que je dit?
mistakes.right: Vous comprenez ce que je dis?
mistakes.why: The embedded clause still takes dis with je.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

cest-il-est.explain: C'est un mot difficile identifies something: c'est followed by a noun phrase with un. Once a masculine thing such as a word or book is identified, il est difficile describes it. C'est difficile is also right when describing the situation or task as a whole. The choice follows what you are identifying or describing; c'est is not forbidden before an adjective.
cest-il-est.why: [[C'est un mot]] identifies the thing. [[Il est difficile]] describes the word already mentioned.

examples.text: Je le comprends, mais c'est difficile.
examples.means: I understand it, but it's difficult.
examples.literal: I it understand, but it's difficult.

contrasts.says: il can refer to a masculine noun such as mot or livre; the pronoun follows the noun's gender.
English can use it's for identifying a thing and for describing it. French uses different constructions.

mistakes.why: ce and est must join as c'est.
With il, the form is est.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

il-y-a.explain: Il y a introduces something present: Il y a une porte ouverte (there's a door open). The same expression is used for there is and there are. The il belongs to the expression; it does not point to a particular man. Learn il y a as a whole.
il-y-a.why: [[Il y a]] introduces what is there; the next words tell you what it is.

examples.text: Il y a une porte ouverte.
Il y a de l'eau sur la table.
examples.literal: There is some water on the table.

contrasts.says: French uses one fixed expression for there is and there are.

mistakes.wrong: Il y as une porte ouverte.
mistakes.right: Il y a une porte ouverte.
mistakes.why: The expression uses a, never the tu form as.

mistakes.wrong: Il y a un porte ouverte.
mistakes.right: Il y a une porte ouverte.
mistakes.why: porte is feminine: une porte.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

adjective-after.explain: ouverte follows porte when describing the open door: la porte ouverte. It also matches the noun: porte is feminine, so ouvert becomes ouverte. Many French adjectives follow the noun. This does not mean every adjective must follow it; learn the position with the adjective.
adjective-after.why: French says la porte [[ouverte]], literally the door open, where English says the open door.

examples.text: Je marche vers la porte ouverte.
examples.means: I'm walking to the open door.
examples.literal: I walk towards the door open.

contrasts.says: ouverte matches the feminine noun porte.
An adjective directly describing a noun normally comes before that noun in English; ouverte follows porte.

mistakes.wrong: Je marche vers la porte ouverts.
mistakes.right: Je marche vers la porte ouverte.
mistakes.why: A single feminine porte takes ouverte.
The adjective must match the singular feminine noun.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

perfect.explain: To say you have lost something, use avoir plus perdu: J'ai perdu ta clé. perdu is the past participle of perdre. The form of avoir changes with the subject: Tu as perdu la clé?; Ils ont perdu la clé. These sentences can describe a past event or its present result. French uses this tense for both I lost and I've lost.
perfect.why: [[J'ai perdu]] has two parts: avoir gives the person, and perdu says what happened.

examples.text: Tu as aussi perdu la clé?
examples.means: Have you lost the key too?
examples.literal: You have also lost the key?

contrasts.says: The auxiliary avoir changes for the person; perdu stays the same in these examples.
This French tense can correspond to I lost or I have lost, depending on the context.

mistakes.why: je joins ai before the vowel.
With ils, avoir is ont.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

on.explain: In everyday conversation, on often means we: On fait du café. It takes the same verb form as il: on fait, on aime, on prépare. Even when several people mean we, do not use a nous ending after on. Outside this we meaning, on can also refer to people in general or an unspecified person; context tells you who is meant.
on.why: [[On fait]] is everyday we make; the verb is still fait, not faisons.

examples.text: On fait du café pour vous.
examples.means: We're making coffee for you all.
examples.literal: We make some coffee for you.

examples.text: On aime manger ensemble à la maison.
examples.means: We like eating together at home.
examples.literal: We like to eat together at the house.

contrasts.says: Nous and on can both refer to we, but their verb forms differ: nous mangeons, on mange.
vous still addresses the listeners, as in On fait du café pour vous.

mistakes.why: on takes the il form fait.
The form after on is prépare, even when it means we.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

avoir.explain: French expresses needing with avoir besoin de: Tu as besoin d'aide? Literally, you have need of help. Change avoir for the person: j'ai besoin, tu as besoin, nous avons besoin. Before aide, de becomes d': d'aide. You can also name a thing needed: Tu as besoin de mon téléphone?
avoir.why: Where English uses need as a verb, French uses [[avoir besoin de]].

examples.text: Nous avons besoin d'aide pour payer.
examples.literal: We have need of help for paying.

examples.text: Tu as besoin de mon téléphone?
examples.literal: You have need of my phone?

contrasts.says: de joins aide as d'aide.
English need takes the thing directly; French avoir besoin takes de before it.

mistakes.why: Use as with tu.
de loses its e before aide.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronoun.explain: te is the person being helped or addressed: Je te pose une question. Put it before the verb. With peux plus an infinitive, put te before the infinitive: Je peux te poser une question? Before a vowel, te becomes t': Je peux t'aider avec le travail. The pronoun belongs with the action it completes.
object-pronoun.why: [[te]] goes before pose; in peux t'aider, [[t']] goes before aider, not after it.

examples.text: Je peux te poser une question?
examples.means: Can I ask you a question?
examples.literal: I can you ask a question?

examples.text: Je peux t'aider avec le travail.
examples.means: I can help you with the work.
examples.literal: I can you help with the work.

contrasts.says: After avec use toi; before the verb as its object use te or t'.
The object pronoun goes with the infinitive it completes: peux t'aider.

mistakes.why: In a statement, te goes before pose.
te loses its e before aider.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

aller.explain: A form of aller followed directly by an infinitive can say what is going to happen: Je vais boire ce café. vais changes for je; boire stays in its basic form. No à goes between aller and the infinitive in this construction. aller can also describe travel to a place: Je vais à la maison.
aller.why: [[Je vais boire]] expresses the next action: I'm going to drink.

examples.means: I'm going to drink this coffee.

examples.text: Je vais à la maison avec ma mère.
examples.means: I'm going home with my mother.
examples.literal: I go to the house with my mother.

contrasts.says: As after vouloir, the second verb is an infinitive.
English going to includes to; French vais boire has no preposition.

mistakes.why: Use the infinitive boire after vais.
With the feminine noun maison, the place is à la maison.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.

contraction.explain: à and the definite article le join as au: au bureau means to the office or at the office. Keep à la before a feminine noun: à la maison. de and le similarly join as du. These joins are required when the preposition is followed by the definite article le; they are not optional spelling choices.
contraction.why: French writes [[au bureau]], never à le bureau.

examples.means: Are you going to the office today?
examples.literal: You go to the office today?

examples.means: I always work at the office.
examples.literal: I work always at the office.

contrasts.says: du also occurs in du café, where it introduces an amount.
French au is one written word where English says at the or to the.

mistakes.wrong: Tu vas à le bureau aujourd'hui?
mistakes.why: à and the definite article le join as au.
maison is feminine: à la stays separate.

source.note: Written with the French lessons 21–40, open to correction.
